beats.headline: Stop blocking your API for a welcome email.
beats.subline: Your HTTP handlers should not wait for side effects. Use events to decouple.
beats.narration: Your API response shouldn't wait for an email to send. If your service is coupled to every side effect, you're building a monolith that's impossible to scale.

beats.title: Publishing Domain Events

steps.explanation: Event publishing happens within the same transaction context.
Decouples the service from listeners like Email or Audit.

beats.narration: Inject the ApplicationEventPublisher. By publishing an immutable record, your OrderService doesn't need to know who is listening or what side effects occur.

beats.title: Sync vs Async Listeners
beats.narration: Default listeners run synchronously on the caller's thread. If you do heavy I/O, use @Async with a dedicated executor to keep your main thread fast.

beats.title: Event Safety
beats.narration: Spring events reside in memory. If a pod dies, the event dies. For critical workflows like payments, use a transactional outbox pattern instead.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next: Fixing the AFTER_COMMIT transaction bug →
beats.narration: That's decoupling. In Part 2, we fix the bug where your database writes inside listeners silently fail to persist.

beats.headline: Why your listener is writing to a dead transaction.
beats.subline: AFTER_COMMIT listeners need a new transaction, or your data won't save.
beats.narration: Ever noticed your listener code runs but nothing hits the database? It's because the transaction already committed before your code finished.

beats.title: Fixing the Commit Race

steps.explanation: Starts a fresh transaction since the original is already closed.
Ensures the event only fires if the DB write actually succeeded.

beats.narration: Use TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT to ensure your logic only runs after the data is safe. And always use REQUIRES_NEW to open a fresh transaction context.

beats.title: Transaction Phases
beats.narration: Choose your phase wisely. AFTER_COMMIT is your default for side effects, while AFTER_ROLLBACK is perfect for alerting if a critical operation fails.

beats.title: The Fallback Trap

lines.text: // Default: ignored if no transaction is active
// Now runs even without a transaction

beats.narration: If your event might be published outside a transaction, set fallbackExecution to true. Otherwise, your listener will silently ignore the event.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next: Preventing cache stampedes with sync=true →
beats.narration: Transaction safety achieved. In Part 3, we stop cache stampedes from crashing your database under high load.

beats.headline: Your cache is a stampede waiting to happen.
beats.subline: When a hot key expires, your DB gets hit by 1000 requests at once.
beats.narration: When a hot cache key expires, your database gets hammered by a thundering herd. Here is how to stop it with one simple flag.

beats.title: Stampede Protection

steps.explanation: Locks the key so only one thread loads from the DB.

beats.narration: Set sync = true on your Cacheable annotation. This locks the key locally, forcing concurrent requests to wait for the first thread to populate the cache.

beats.title: Redis Config Best Practices
beats.narration: Never use default JDK serialization. It creates opaque binary blobs. Use Jackson JSON serialization so you can actually debug your data in Redis.

beats.title: Proxy Bypass Warning
beats.narration: Spring caching uses AOP proxies. If you call a cached method via 'this' inside the same bean, the proxy is bypassed and caching never happens.

beats.narration: Cache optimized. In Part 4, we finish with clustered scheduling so your jobs don't run 5 times on 5 pods.

beats.headline: Why your cron job is running 5 times.
beats.subline: Scheduled tasks are local to the JVM. Here is how to coordinate them across pods.
beats.narration: Deploying 5 pods means your cron job runs 5 times. That's a disaster for billing or cleanup jobs. Here is how to lock them down.

beats.title: ShedLock Coordination

steps.explanation: Acquires a DB lock so only one pod executes the job.

beats.narration: ShedLock uses a shared database table to coordinate. Only the pod that wins the lock runs the job; the others skip it silently.

beats.title: Scheduler Thread Pool

lines.text: # Now tasks don't starve each other

beats.narration: Spring's default scheduler pool is size 1. If one task hangs, everything else stops. Always increase your pool size in production.

beats.title: Lock Bounds
beats.narration: Use lockAtLeastFor to prevent overlapping due to clock drift, and lockAtMostFor to ensure the lock releases if a pod crashes mid-job.
